commands.desc: Set the setuid bit on a file
commands.tooltip: Setuid means the file runs with the privileges of its owner, not the user who launches it. The s replaces the owner execute bit and shows as rws in ls -l. The kernel ignores setuid on shell scripts, so this only works on compiled binaries and carries real security risk.

commands.desc: Set the setgid bit on a directory
commands.tooltip: Setgid on a directory makes new files created inside it inherit the directory's group instead of the creator's primary group. This is the classic trick for team-shared folders. It shows as rwxr-sr-x in ls -l and pairs with group ACLs.

commands.desc: Set the sticky bit on a directory
commands.tooltip: The sticky bit means only the file owner, the directory owner, or root can delete files inside the directory, no matter who has write access. /tmp is the classic example and shows a t in the last permission position. Run chmod +t on shared drop folders to stop users deleting each other's files.

The leading 4 in the four-digit mode sets the setuid bit while 755 grants the owner rwx and everyone else rx. Numeric chmod 4755 is the exact same as chmod u+s plus chmod 755 in one step. Remove the bit with chmod u-s or chmod 0755, and audit setuid files with find / -perm -4000.

The +a flag makes a file append-only, so processes can add lines but nothing can overwrite or delete existing content, not even root. This is ideal for audit logs that must stay tamper-proof. Reverse it with sudo chattr -a.

The +i flag makes a file completely immutable, so even root cannot modify, rename, or delete it until the flag is removed. This hardens critical files like /etc/hosts or /etc/passwd against accidental edits and malware. Reverse it with sudo chattr -i and list attributes with lsattr.

commands.desc: List extended attributes of a directory
commands.tooltip: lsattr shows the ext filesystem attributes such as i for immutable and a for append-only. The -d flag lists the directory itself rather than descending into its contents, like ls -d does. Use lsattr -R to walk a whole tree.

An ACL (access control list) grants permissions to extra users and groups beyond the classic owner, group, and other bits. getfacl prints the base mode plus every named user and group entry, and -R walks all subdirectories. Look for the mask line, which caps what the named entries can receive.

commands.desc: Grant a group read and execute ACL
commands.tooltip: setfacl -m modifies an ACL in place, and the g:devs:rx argument gives the group devs read and execute rights without touching the base mode. The colon syntax is scope:name:permissions, so u:alice:rw would target a single user. Existing entries are overwritten, not duplicated.

Adding -R makes setfacl walk every file and directory under /srv/shared, applying the g:devs:rx entry everywhere. This is the efficient way to open up a whole project tree to one group. Files created later do not inherit the entry unless the directory also carries a default ACL.

The -x flag deletes one named entry from the ACL instead of modifying values. Here it strips the group devs entry from /srv/shared while leaving every other entry untouched. Verify the result with getfacl.

The mask entry is the ceiling for what named users and groups can actually use, so m::rx caps every named entry at read and execute even if one was granted write. Tighten the mask to block group access without deleting the entries themselves. The mask only limits named entries, never the file owner.

commands.desc: Remove all capabilities from a file
commands.tooltip: Capabilities are fine-grained privileges like cap_net_bind_service that let a binary bind low ports without full root. The -r flag deletes every capability from the file, restoring normal execution. Audit what is set with getcap -r / 2>/dev/null.

commands.desc: Show the SELinux context of a file
commands.tooltip: The -Z flag prints the SELinux security context column, which labels each file with a type such as etc_t or shadow_t. SELinux is the mandatory access control system used on RHEL and Fedora, and Ubuntu systems show an empty column instead. Pair it with getenforce to see whether SELinux is enforcing.

commands.desc: Copy ownership from a reference file
commands.tooltip: The --reference form copies the user and group of template.txt onto report.pdf instead of typing a user:group pair. This is handy when a file was restored or extracted with the wrong owner. The same reference trick exists in chmod --reference for permissions.

This is how a Linux system selects its timezone: /etc/localtime is a symlink into the IANA zoneinfo database, so no file is copied. Read the link with readlink /etc/localtime to see the chosen zone. Prefer timedatectl set-timezone, which manages this link for you.

readlink resolves a symlink and prints where it actually points. Without -f it shows only one level, so the /etc/alternatives link reveals the real interpreter binary. Add -f to keep resolving until a final non-link path is reached.

commands.desc: Resolve a path to its absolute form
commands.tooltip: realpath prints the canonical absolute path, resolving symlinks and collapsing .. segments along the way. It answers questions like where this script really lives when launched through a symlink. Use it in scripts before cd-ing or storing paths.

commands.desc: Resolve a path without requiring existence
commands.tooltip: The -m flag canonicalizes a path purely by string logic, so the target does not need to exist on disk. This is useful for building paths that a program will create later. Symlinks are not resolved in this mode.

commands.desc: Print file type, size, and mtime
commands.tooltip: stat -c takes a custom format string: %F is the file type, %s the size in bytes, and %y the last modification time with full precision. It is the fastest way to get exactly the fields a script needs. See stat --help for the full format specifier list.

The -f flag switches stat from file details to the underlying filesystem: type, block size, and free blocks. It is the quick way to check what filesystem a path lives on and how much space remains. Compare with df, which shows the same data in human units.

commands.desc: Print the MIME type of a file
commands.tooltip: MIME types are the standard labels such as application/pdf that identify a file's format. The --mime-type flag prints just the type, while plain file adds a human description and -i includes the charset. file inspects magic bytes, not extensions, so it works on renamed files.

The -z flag makes file peek inside compressed archives and report what the decompressed data really is. It detects gzip, bzip2, zip, and other containers automatically. Useful for checking whether a download is a tarball or something else entirely.

basename strips the directory part and prints file.txt, the final component of the path. It is the standard tool for pulling a filename out of a full path in scripts. Pair it with dirname to get the directory half.

commands.desc: Strip a suffix from the basename
commands.tooltip: The -s flag removes a trailing suffix, so this prints just file instead of file.txt. Scripts use it to derive output names from inputs, like turning report.txt into report.pdf. The suffix is matched literally at the end of the name.

commands.desc: Print the directory portion of a path
commands.tooltip: dirname prints everything before the last component, so this yields /path/to. It is the inverse of basename and together they split any path into its two halves. Scripts commonly wrap it around realpath to get an absolute directory.

commands.desc: Show every location of a command
commands.tooltip: The -a flag lists every match for python3 across PATH, not just the first one. This reveals shadowed installations where one binary hides another. Plain which stops at the first hit, which is the one the shell would actually run.

commands.desc: Show how the shell resolves a command
commands.tooltip: type tells you whether a name is an alias, a function, a builtin, or an external binary. The -a flag prints every definition in lookup order, so you see both the alias and the /usr/bin/ls it expands to. Use it before debugging why a command behaves unexpectedly.

commands.desc: Print the path a command would run
commands.tooltip: command -v is the POSIX-standard way to ask which binary the shell would execute, and unlike which it understands aliases and builtins. For a builtin like cd it prints the name itself instead of a path. Scripts use it to locate tools before calling them.

commands.desc: Clear the shell's command hash table
commands.tooltip: Bash caches the PATH lookup for every command it runs, and hash -r forgets that cache so the next call re-searches PATH. Run it after installing a new binary that shadows an old one, or after moving executables. Plain hash lists the cached entries.

commands.desc: Format a number with zero padding
commands.tooltip: printf is the shell's formatted output builtin, and %05d pads the number 42 to five digits with leading zeros, printing 00042. The same format specifiers as C and Python apply, so %x gives hex and %.2f fixes decimals. It is more predictable than echo for scripted output.

The -n limit controls how many file descriptors one shell session may hold, and this raises the soft limit to 4096. The soft limit can be raised only up to the hard limit, which needs root to increase. Set it in ~/.bashrc or a systemd unit for persistence.

commands.desc: Show the max user processes limit
commands.tooltip: The -u limit caps how many processes and threads a single user may run, and this prints the current value. Hitting it produces fork: Cannot allocate memory errors despite plenty of RAM. Raise it with ulimit -u or in /etc/security/limits.conf.

ulimit -a dumps every soft limit for the current shell: open files, core dumps, stack size, CPU time, and process count. It is the first stop when a program dies with mysterious resource errors. Each line maps to a single-letter flag like -n or -u.

commands.desc: Run a program in a new session
commands.tooltip: setsid starts the program in a fresh session with no controlling terminal, so terminal close and SIGHUP do not kill it. Unlike a plain background job, it fully detaches from the login session. Pair it with nohup or systemd-run for long-running tasks.

commands.desc: Remove all jobs from the shell's job table
commands.tooltip: disown detaches background jobs from the shell so they survive your logout without receiving SIGHUP. The -a form removes every job at once, while plain disown %1 targets one. Use it after starting a long task with the background operator.

commands.desc: Wait for the next background job to finish
commands.tooltip: wait -n blocks until any one of the shell's background jobs completes and then returns its status, available since Bash 5.1. It lets a script run several jobs in parallel and reap them as they finish. Plain wait with no argument waits for all of them.

commands.desc: Send a TERM signal to a process
commands.tooltip: The -s flag names the signal explicitly, so this politely asks process 1234 to terminate and gives it a chance to clean up. TERM is the default signal and the first choice; escalate to kill -9 only if the process ignores it. List signal names with kill -l.

commands.desc: Terminate every process owned by a user
commands.tooltip: killall -u alice sends TERM to all of alice's processes at once, effectively logging her out and discarding unsaved work. This is a blunt instrument, so check who is affected with pgrep -u alice first. Add -9 to force-kill anything that ignores TERM.

commands.desc: Kill processes by exact name match
commands.tooltip: The -x flag makes pkill match the process name exactly instead of as a substring, so nginx matches only nginx. Plain pkill nginx would also hit processes like nginx-cache. Use pgrep first to preview what will be killed.

pgrep -c prints how many running processes match the name nginx instead of their PIDs. A count of zero also means pgrep exits nonzero, which is handy in script conditions. Combine with -f to match against the full command line.

renice changes the nice value of a running process, and negative values mean higher priority, so -5 boosts process 1234. Raising priority requires root, while lowering it is allowed for your own processes. Revert with renice -n 0 -p 1234 and watch impact with top.

commands.desc: Set a process to idle I/O class
commands.tooltip: ionice controls disk I/O priority, and class 3 means idle, so process 1234 only touches the disk when nobody else needs it. This is perfect for overnight backups that must not slow down interactive work. Classes are 0 none, 1 realtime, 2 best-effort, and 3 idle.

Best-effort class 2 is the default, and the -n level from 0 to 7 tunes priority within it, where 4 sits in the middle. Lower numbers get the disk first, so a compile job at -n 0 would starve everything else. Combine with nice for CPU plus I/O tuning.

commands.desc: Pin a process to specific CPUs
commands.tooltip: taskset sets CPU affinity, and -c 0,1 restricts the new process to the first two CPU cores. Pinning improves cache locality for latency-sensitive workloads and contains noisy neighbors on shared boxes. Verify placement with taskset -pc on the PID.

commands.desc: Move a running process to a CPU
commands.tooltip: The -pc form operates on an existing process, so this migrates process 1234 onto CPU 2 without restarting it. It prints the old and new affinity lists on success. Use it when a process ends up on a busy core and you cannot stop it.

The -V flag understands version numbers, so 1.10 sorts after 1.9 instead of before it as plain lexicographic sort would do. It handles dotted numbers and suffixes like rc1 sensibly. Use it to order release tags and package versions.

commands.desc: Sort a CSV by a numeric column
commands.tooltip: The -t, flag sets the field delimiter to a comma, and -k2,2nr sorts by field 2 with n for numeric and r for reverse order. The start,end key range form -k2,2 pins the sort to exactly one field. Extend the range like -k2,3 to break ties with a second column.

commands.desc: Extract specific fields from a file
commands.tooltip: cut -d: sets the delimiter to a colon and -f1,3 keeps only the first and third fields, so /etc/passwd yields username and UID pairs. Field lists accept ranges such as 2-5 and commas mixed with ranges. Pair with sort or uniq to analyze columnar data.

commands.desc: Strip carriage returns from a file
commands.tooltip: The -d flag deletes characters, so this removes every carriage return from a Windows CRLF file, leaving clean Unix line endings. Feed the result to a new file with a redirect instead of printing it. The same trick fixes files that show ^M in editors.

POSIX character classes in brackets handle locale-aware ranges, so [:upper:] maps cleanly to [:lower:] for any alphabet. This is more reliable than tr A-Z a-z for accented letters. Read from a file with the input redirect and write with an output redirect.

commands.desc: Join two CSVs keeping unmatched rows
commands.tooltip: join merges two sorted files on a key column, here field 1 of both, and -a 1 keeps every row from the first file even without a match in the second. The process substitution runs each sort as a virtual file, satisfying join's sorted-input requirement. Without -a, unmatched rows are dropped silently.

commands.desc: Show lines unique to the second file
commands.tooltip: comm compares two sorted files and prints three columns: lines only in the first, only in the second, and in both. The -13 flag suppresses the first two columns so only lines unique to b.txt remain. The reverse filter comm -23 shows lines only in a.txt.

commands.desc: Split a file into fixed-size chunks
commands.tooltip: The -b flag splits by size, producing part_aa, part_ab, and so on, each 10 megabytes except the last. Splitting helps upload large files through size-limited channels. Reassemble in order with cat part_* > bigfile.

commands.desc: Split a file at matching lines
commands.tooltip: csplit cuts a file wherever a line matches the pattern, so '/^Chapter/' starts a new part at each chapter heading and '{*}' repeats the split for every match. The -f flag sets the prefix and -b '%02d.txt' formats the numeric suffixes. Unlike split, the parts differ in size.

The -L flag reports the length of the longest line in characters instead of counting lines or words. It is handy for checking whether any line overflows a fixed-width report or terminal column. Combine with sort -n to rank line lengths across many files.

commands.desc: Print all but the last five lines
commands.tooltip: A negative count flips head around, so -n -5 prints every line except the final five. This is the mirror of tail -n -5 and handy when the end of a file contains a footer you want to exclude. The feature needs the explicit -n form.

commands.desc: Print a sequence with zero padding
commands.tooltip: seq prints consecutive numbers, and -w pads them to equal width, giving 01 through 10 instead of 1 through 10. This keeps filenames and columns sorting correctly in scripts. Add a step like seq 1 2 99 to count odd numbers.

commands.desc: Pick random numbers from a range
commands.tooltip: The -i flag turns shuf into a random number generator for the inclusive range 1 to 100, and -n 5 prints five distinct picks. Without -n it shuffles the whole range. For random lines from a file, pass the filename instead of -i.

nl prepends line numbers in the classic cat -n style, and -ba numbers every line, including empty ones, instead of skipping them. The default skips blank lines unless -ba is given. Tune the format with -w for width and -s for the separator.

commands.desc: Dump binary with hex offsets and ASCII
commands.tooltip: od is the octal dump utility, and -A x switches addresses to hex while -t x1z prints each byte in hex followed by printable ASCII in the margin. This is the fastest way to eyeball binary file contents. Plain od -c shows bytes as escaped characters.

commands.desc: Export a file as a C array
commands.tooltip: The -i flag formats the file as an initialized C array named after the input, ready to embed in source code. This is the standard way to bundle small assets like icons into a binary. Add a length variable with -i plus -l to cap the size.

commands.desc: Show a canonical hex and ASCII dump
commands.tooltip: The -C flag is the canonical hexdump layout, showing offset, sixteen hex bytes, and the printable ASCII column. It is the tool of choice for inspecting binary files and network captures. Compare with od -A x -t x1z, which produces a similar view.

sha256sum prints the 64-character SHA-256 digest of a file, the standard way to verify a download matches the publisher's checksum. Compare the output against the value on the official download page. The same digest confirms two files are identical.

The -c flag reads a manifest of hash plus filename lines and verifies each file, printing OK or FAILED per line. A FAILED line means the file was corrupted or tampered with. Generate the manifest itself with sha256sum file > SHA256SUMS.

md5sum prints the 32-character MD5 digest of a file. MD5 is fast but cryptographically broken, so use it only for quick integrity checks, never for security. Prefer sha256sum whenever authenticity matters.

base64 converts binary data into the printable base64 alphabet so it survives email and JSON transport. It prints the encoded text to stdout, ready to redirect to a file. The encoding inflates size by roughly a third.

The -d flag reverses the encoding and restores the original bytes, so a file encoded with base64 comes back intact. Add -i to ignore invalid characters in sloppy input. This is how base64-encoded attachments and config blobs are unpacked.

fold wraps lines longer than the width, and -s breaks at spaces instead of splitting words in half. The -w flag sets the width, here 40 columns. This formats plain text for narrow terminals or email without a full text formatter.

rev mirrors every line, so hello becomes olleh, useful for right-aligning text or trick questions. It is often chained with sort to find lines that share reversed endings. Character order reverses but lines stay in place.

pr paginates and columns text for printing, and the -2 flag lays the file out in two side-by-side columns. The -t flag suppresses the page headers and footers, keeping only the data. Column counts like -4 work for wide listings.

gsettings reads and writes the DConf settings database through the session's DBus, and this fetches the current wallpaper URI. Keys are addressed as schema plus key name, here the background schema's picture-uri. The value prints in GVariant syntax with quotes.

This sets the wallpaper by writing the picture-uri key, and single quotes protect the file URI from shell expansion. The change applies to the running session immediately with no restart. Use dconf read to confirm the stored value.

commands.desc: Dump all keys in a schema
commands.tooltip: list-recursively prints every key in the interface schema with its current value, one per line. A schema is a named group of related settings, and this is the fastest way to discover what is configurable. Pair it with gsettings range to see a key's allowed values.

This sets the GTK theme for GNOME applications, with Adwaita-dark being the built-in dark theme. Installed third-party themes appear as new options in the same key. The change applies live to most running GTK apps.

The text-scaling-factor key multiplies all on-screen text, and 1.25 enlarges it by a quarter for easier reading. The valid range is 0.5 to 3.0, checkable with gsettings range. This is the accessibility-friendly alternative to lowering the whole display resolution.

monitor subscribes to a schema and prints every key change as it happens, ideal for seeing what an app or setting dialog modifies. It runs until Ctrl+C. The same trick works on a single key path for narrower output.

commands.desc: Back up GNOME settings to a file
commands.tooltip: dconf is the low-level settings database behind gsettings, and dump writes an entire subtree as readable keyfile text. The redirect saves it to gnome-backup.conf for later restore. Dump the whole /org/gnome/ tree to capture every GNOME app's settings.

commands.desc: Restore GNOME settings from a backup
commands.tooltip: load reads a keyfile from stdin and writes every key back into the database, the exact inverse of dconf dump. Keys present in the file are overwritten, so this restores a full backup in one shot. Run it while logged into the same session so apps pick up the changes.

commands.desc: Watch a settings path for changes
commands.tooltip: watch prints every write to keys under the given path as it happens, showing the key and its new value. It is the raw DConf-level equivalent of gsettings monitor and catches changes from any source. Press Ctrl+C to stop.

The -f flag makes reset recurse, returning every key under /org/gnome/desktop/ to its factory default in one command. This is irreversible for custom settings, so dump a backup first. The same flag resets whole apps when pointed at their paths.

dconf read prints a single key's value using the raw path form, with slash-separated schema and key names. It is the direct database access behind gsettings get. The output uses GVariant syntax, so strings appear quoted.

GNOME Shell extensions are JavaScript add-ons that alter the desktop, identified by UUIDs like ubuntu-appindicators@ubuntu.com. The --enabled filter shows only active ones, while plain list shows everything installed. Pipe to grep for a specific extension.

This turns off the Ubuntu AppIndicators extension by its UUID, and the desktop reacts immediately without a shell restart. Disabling keeps the files installed, so the extension can be enabled again later. Use gnome-extensions list --enabled first to confirm the UUID.

This reactivates a disabled or freshly installed extension by UUID. The change applies to the current session at once. If it still does not appear, log out and back in so the shell reloads its extension set.

commands.desc: Show details of a Shell extension
commands.tooltip: info prints an extension's name, version, description, and current state such as enabled or error. The state field is the first place to check when an extension misbehaves. A broken extension shows ERROR here and may need a reset.

commands.desc: Move a file to the trash
commands.tooltip: gio is the GLib command-line front end to GVfs, and trash moves a file into the desktop trash instead of deleting it. The file can be restored from the file manager's trash view, so this is the safe delete. Trash lives in ~/.local/share/Trash.
This deletes every file in the trash for good, freeing the disk space they occupied. There is no undo, so check the trash first. The flag is --empty, not --empty-trash.

commands.desc: Open a file with the default application
commands.tooltip: gio open launches the default application registered for the file's MIME type, exactly like double-clicking in the file manager. It respects the same associations as xdg-open. From a terminal it works with any MIME-registered file type.

gio info prints attributes such as size, type, permissions, and modification time, plus trash status for trashed files. It reads the same GVfs metadata layer the file manager uses. Add -a with attribute names to filter the output.

gio list prints the contents of a location through the GVfs layer, which also understands remote schemes like sftp:// and trash://. It is ls for anything the file manager can open. Use -a attributes to request metadata columns.

xrandr is the X11 RandR extension client, and running it bare lists every output with its supported resolutions and refresh rates. Output names like HDMI-1 and eDP-1 come from the left column. It only works on X11 sessions, not Wayland.

The --output flag names a display and --mode picks one of its supported resolutions, so this switches HDMI-1 to 1080p. The mode must appear in the plain xrandr listing. Add --rate to also set the refresh rate.

The --rate flag sets the refresh in hertz, and this asks HDMI-1 to run at 144 Hz for smoother motion. The monitor must support the rate at the current resolution, or xrandr refuses. Combine it in the same command as --mode for a precise mode plus rate pair.

commands.desc: Position a display left of another
commands.tooltip: Relative position flags arrange outputs on the virtual desktop, so eDP-1 sits to the left of HDMI-1 and the mouse moves between them naturally. Siblings include --right-of, --above, and --below. The arrangement persists only for the current X session.
The primary output is where new windows and panels appear by default on X11. This marks HDMI-1 as primary while the others stay secondary. Only one output can be primary at a time.

This disables the HDMI-1 output, mirroring the settings panel's display off toggle. Turning off the only active monitor blanks the screen, so have a fallback ready. Re-enable it with xrandr --output HDMI-1 --auto.

xset configures the X server directly, and the s command controls the screensaver, so s off disables it entirely. The setting lasts until the X session ends or the server restarts. Pair with xset dpms to also control display power saving.

The dpms command sets the Display Power Management Signaling delays in seconds for standby, suspend, and off. This sequence powers the monitor down after ten minutes of inactivity. Pass 0 0 0 to disable power saving entirely.

The q flag queries the X server and prints screensaver, DPMS, keyboard, and pointer settings in one dump. It is the fastest way to see what the server is actually configured to do. Look at the DPMS and screensaver sections to confirm prior xset changes.

wlr-randr manages displays on wlroots-based Wayland compositors, the Wayland world's answer to xrandr. Wayland is the modern display protocol replacing X11, and this tool talks to its output-management protocol. Bare wlr-randr lists outputs, resolutions, and refresh rates.

This configures the DP-1 output on a wlroots compositor, with the mode given as width, height, and refresh rate joined by an at sign. The @60 sets the hertz; omitting it keeps the current rate. Add --scale 1.5 for HiDPI scaling.

pactl talks to the PulseAudio sound server, and info prints the server version, default sink, and default source. PulseAudio is the classic Linux sound daemon, now often bridged to PipeWire. The default sink name here is what set-default-sink expects.

A sink is an audio output device, and the short form prints a terse table of sinks with names and states, perfect for scripting. The first column contains the full names used by set-default-sink. Drop short for the verbose per-sink detail dump.

The @DEFAULT_SINK@ token stands for whatever sink is currently the default, and 80% sets the volume as a percentage. Volumes also accept linear factors like 0.8 or decibel values. A leading plus or minus adjusts relative to the current level.
This makes the named ALSA sink the default, so new playback streams route there. The exact sink name comes from pactl list sinks short. Switching between speakers and headphones is the classic use.

module-null-sink creates a virtual sink that accepts audio but plays nothing, useful for recording application output or routing experiments. The command prints the new module's numeric index, which unload-module expects. Remove it with pactl unload-module followed by that index.

commands.desc: Toggle mute on the default output
commands.tooltip: This flips the mute state of the default sink between muted and unmuted, the command-line version of the volume menu's mute button. The third argument also accepts 1 for mute and 0 for unmute. The change is immediate for all streams on that sink.

pw-cli is the low-level admin console for PipeWire, the modern audio and video server on most desktops. info all prints every global object with its properties, from devices to link nodes. The output is dense, so grep for a specific interface type.

The ls command lists objects, and filtering by the Node interface shows audio devices, virtual sinks, and streams. Each entry carries an object id used by other pw-cli commands. PipeWire nodes are the building blocks of the audio graph.

commands.desc: List PipeWire node names as JSON
commands.tooltip: pw-dump prints the entire PipeWire state as JSON, and the jq filter extracts just the node.name property of every Node object. This is the script-friendly way to enumerate audio devices. The same dump feeds any jq query for graph inspection.

wpctl is the control tool for WirePlumber, the session manager that wires PipeWire devices together. status prints the audio graph with sinks, sources, and their default markers. The numbered ids shown here are what set-volume and friends accept.

This sets the default audio sink's volume to 0.8, meaning 80 percent, and @DEFAULT_AUDIO_SINK@ is the magic name for the current default. The value accepts fractions, percentages like 80%, and relative adjustments with a plus or minus. The same command works with a numeric sink id.

get-volume prints the current volume of the default sink, such as Volume: 0.80. It is the quick sanity check before scripting volume changes. The id argument can be the magic default name or any sink id from wpctl status.

The --user flag targets the per-user systemd instance instead of the system-wide one, so this checks the PipeWire service running under your session. User services live in ~/.config/systemd/user and start at login. Status shows active or failed plus recent log lines.

This restarts the PipeWire service inside your user session, picking up config changes without a reboot. Restarting audio services briefly cuts sound and can reset volume levels. The same pattern manages any user unit, from syncthing to podman socket activation.

commands.desc: Show recent logs for a user service
commands.tooltip: journalctl --user restricts the log view to your session's services, and -u pipewire filters to that unit while -n 20 keeps the last twenty lines. This is the first stop when a desktop service misbehaves. Add -f to follow new messages live.

commands.desc: Show details of an installed Flatpak
commands.tooltip: Flatpak distributes sandboxed apps identified by reverse-DNS ids like org.gimp.GIMP, and info prints the installed version, origin remote, and runtime. The runtime line shows which shared platform the app depends on. Compare with flatpak list for a summary table.
flatpak ps shows every Flatpak app currently running, with its instance id and application id. The instance id is what flatpak kill expects. If nothing is listed, no sandboxed apps are open.

Runtimes are the shared dependency platforms that Flatpak apps are built against, and this removes every runtime no installed app needs anymore. It is the single best disk-space reclaim for Flatpak systems. The command lists what it would remove and asks before deleting.

This politely terminates the running GIMP instance managed by Flatpak, equivalent to closing the app normally. Unlike killing the process tree by hand, it goes through the sandbox instance. Use flatpak ps to confirm the app is actually running first.

Snaps can bundle background daemons, and snap services prints each one with its startup setting and current state. Service names follow the snap name, like nextcloud.nextcloud-cron. Control them with snap start, stop, and restart.

snap changes lists every snap operation with an id, status, and timestamp, from installs to refreshes. A long-running change can be followed with snap change followed by its id. Failed changes show a red error status worth investigating.

This tells snapd to keep just two revisions of each snap, down from the default three, freeing disk space on snap-heavy systems. Older revisions are what snap revert rolls back to, so a smaller retain window means fewer rollback options. Read the current value with snap get system refresh.retain.

snap get reads configuration keys from the snapd store, and this prints the current refresh.retain value. It confirms whether a snap set change actually took effect. Other useful keys live under the refresh and proxy namespaces.

update-alternatives manages symlink groups where several programs compete, like the editor group pointing /etc/alternatives/editor at one binary. The --set form pins the choice non-interactively, ideal for scripts and image builds. List the group's candidates with --list first.

The --auto flag returns the editor group to automatic mode, where the alternative with the highest priority wins. This undoes a manual --set choice and lets package upgrades re-decide the default. Automatic status shows as auto in --display output.

--config shows a numbered menu of every candidate in the editor group and applies the one you choose. It is the interactive counterpart to --set. The menu also reveals the current selection and each candidate's priority.

--list prints every binary registered in the editor group, one path per line, without needing root. It is the read-only way to see what a --config menu would offer. Each entry is a real executable registered via --install.

adduser is the friendly Debian wrapper around useradd, prompting for a password and full name as it creates the account. It also builds the home directory and copies in the default skeleton files. The interactive prompts can be skipped with flags like --disabled-password.

commands.desc: Add an existing user to a group
commands.tooltip: The adduser USER GROUP form adds an existing user to an existing group, here granting alice sudo privileges. The user must log out and back in for the new group to take effect. It is the interactive equivalent of usermod -aG.

commands.desc: Create a user without a password
commands.tooltip: The --disabled-password flag creates the account with no password, so it cannot log in interactively until one is set, and --comment '' skips the full-name prompt. This is the standard recipe for service accounts. Lock it down further with --shell /usr/sbin/nologin.

deluser removes alice's account but leaves her home directory and files on disk. Remove those too with deluser --remove-home, or --remove-all-files for files owned elsewhere. Back up anything needed first, since group memberships and ownership records are gone for good.

commands.desc: Delete a user and their home directory
commands.tooltip: The --remove-home flag deletes the account and its home directory together, freeing the disk space immediately. This is irreversible, so confirm nothing important lives in /home/alice first. For a full sweep add --remove-all-files to catch files owned in other directories.

A group is a named set of users that shares permissions, and groupadd creates one, here developers. The system assigns the next free GID automatically. Assign users to it with usermod -aG or adduser USER GROUP.

commands.desc: Create a group with a fixed GID
commands.tooltip: The -g flag pins the group's GID to 1500 instead of letting the system choose, useful when NFS or config files expect a specific number. Check existing GIDs with getent group first to avoid collisions. The same -g flag works for useradd.

commands.desc: Look up a group in NSS
commands.tooltip: getent queries the NSS (name service switch) databases that back user and group lookups, so this shows the developers group's GID and members. It sees accounts from /etc/passwd, LDAP, and NIS alike. Use it to verify a groupadd or usermod took effect.

commands.desc: Look up a service port in NSS
commands.tooltip: The services database maps service names to port numbers, so this prints ssh 22/tcp. getent services is the reliable way to look up standard ports without guessing. The same getent command works on passwd, group, and hosts entries.

commands.desc: Force a password change at next login
commands.tooltip: chage manages password aging, and -d 0 sets the last-change date to the epoch, so alice must set a new password on her next login. It is the standard way to expire a password immediately. Peek at the full aging policy with chage -l alice.

The -S flag prints the account's password status: L for locked, P for a usable password, and NP for no password at all. The output also shows the last change date and aging policy. Use it before locking or unlocking accounts to see where they stand.

commands.desc: Add a user to a group
commands.tooltip: usermod -aG appends alice to the developers group, and the -a flag is essential because plain -G replaces her entire group list. New group membership needs a fresh login to apply. Verify with groups alice or getent group developers.

commands.desc: Disable shell login for a user
commands.tooltip: Setting the login shell to nologin means alice cannot open an interactive shell, though her other services and file access keep working. This is the clean way to lock down a service account without deleting it. Reverse it with usermod -s /bin/bash alice.
The GECOS field holds the account's real name and contact info, and -c sets it, here to Alice Smith. This is what finger and some login screens display. Quote the value so spaces survive the shell.

The -D flag prints the defaults useradd applies to new accounts: base home directory, default shell, skeleton, and expiry policy. These defaults live in /etc/default/useradd. Root can override individual defaults with useradd -D -s /bin/bash.

The -r flag creates a system account with a UID below 1000, and -s /usr/sbin/nologin blocks interactive login, the standard recipe for daemons. System accounts skip the normal home directory creation unless -m is added. Use adduser for interactive human accounts instead.

lastb reads /var/log/btmp and lists failed login attempts with usernames and source addresses, so it is the first stop when investigating break-in attempts. Reading btmp needs root, hence sudo. The output can be noisy, so pipe it through sort uniq -c to spot brute-force patterns.

The -x flag adds system shutdown, reboot, and runlevel-change entries to last's usual login listing. It reconstructs the machine's boot and power history at a glance. Combine with last reboot to isolate just the reboot events.

commands.desc: Show one user's sessions and activity
commands.tooltip: w with a username limits the report to that user's sessions, showing login time, idle duration, and the command each terminal runs. The WHAT column reveals whether alice is idle or actively working. Bare w covers everyone logged in.

commands.desc: Show one property of a session
commands.tooltip: loginctl talks to systemd-logind, the session manager, and show-session prints properties of session 2. The -p State filter limits output to that one property, here whether the session is active. Find session numbers with loginctl list-sessions.

commands.desc: End all sessions of a user
commands.tooltip: This force-ends every login session alice has, killing her processes and discarding unsaved work. It is the systemd-native way to log a user out, stronger than just closing terminals. Check what she runs with w or ps -u alice first.

list-users shows every user with an active session, their UID, and whether linger is enabled. Linger lets services keep running after logout. The user list pairs with loginctl list-sessions to map sessions to users.

This asks systemd-logind to lock the session, triggering the configured screen locker immediately. It is the command-line equivalent of the Super+L shortcut. No argument locks the caller's own session; a session id targets a specific one.

timedatectl list-timezones dumps every IANA timezone name, and the grep filters it down to matches like Europe/Madrid. Timezone names are region/city pairs that avoid the ambiguities of UTC offsets. Feed the exact result to timedatectl set-timezone.

The locale controls language, date formats, and character encoding for system services, and this sets the primary LANG to Spanish. New sessions inherit the change while running ones keep their old locale. The locale must exist in localectl list-locales or it will be rejected.

list-locales prints every locale the system can actually use, and the grep filters for the Spanish ones. Only locales shown here can be selected with set-locale. Generate missing ones with locale-gen or dpkg-reconfigure locales.
